title: Femme arrangeant des fleurs
description: Femme arrangeant des fleurs signed and dated 'Marie Laurencin 1931' (upper right) oil on canvas 21 5/8 x 18 1/8 in (55 x 46 cm) Painted in 1931
provenance: Galerie Paul Rosenberg, Paris, no. 2927. | Sale: Parke-Bernet, New York, December 16, 1970, lot 91. | Acquired at the above sale by the previous owner. | Thence by descent to the present owner. | | Exhibited | London, The Mayor Gallery, Flower Paintings by Marie Laurencin, December 1934, no. 4. | Paris, Galerie Paul Rosenberg, Marie Laurencin, 1936. | | Literature | D. Marchesseau, Marie Laurencin 1883-1956, Catalogue Raisonné de l'Oeuvre Peint, Tokyo, 1986, no. 535 (illustrated p. 237). | | | French artist Marie Laurencin was synonymous with the Avant Garde for over two decades, yet her highly unique painterly style was one that defied categorization. While Laurencin moved within the intimate circles of artists and intellectuals associated with Fauvism, Dadaism, and Cubism, she repudiated the countless attempts to compartmentalize her art within the restrictive parameters of a certain style or movement. Laurencin refused to compromise with reality and instead painted her vision of a poetic, graceful world inhabited entirely by beautiful young women and animals. This ability to resist conforming to the pressures that surrounded her resulted in a unique, highly distinctive oeuvre and was arguably one of her greatest assets as an artist. | | Femme arrangeant des fleurs, painted in 1931, was produced after Laurencin had reached the mature style most typically associated with her works. This painting's depiction of a girl in an idyllic, floral landscape and its color scheme of pink, pale blue, white, and viridian make it instantly recognizable as the style that characterized Laurencin's work from the 1920s onward. Through its pastel colors and arabesque lines, Femme arrangeant des fleurs conjures a feminine world of lyrical melancholy. Rather than adhering to stylistic considerations, this world is achieved through a preoccupation with the ephemeral, subtle evocations of mood, and sparks of poetry.

title: L'Enfant au tablier blanc
material: oil on canvas laid down on board
description: L'Enfant au tablier blanc signed 'HE Cross' (lower right) oil on canvas laid down on board 16 1/8 x 13 in (41 x 33 cm) Painted circa 1902-1905
provenance: (possibly) Galerie Druet, Paris (acquired from the artist). | Oscar Ghez Collection, Geneva, by 1964; his sale, Versailles, Hôtel Rameau, October 24, 1976, lot 65. | Petit Palais Collection, Geneva, by 1980. | Whitford & Hughes Ltd., London, no. 5007, by 1984; their sale, Sotheby's, London, June 26, 1985, lot 153. | Acquired at the above sale by the present owner. | | Exhibited | Turin, Galleria civica d'arte moderna, 80 Pittori da Renoir à Kisling, February 7 - April 5, 1964, no. 56. | Tel Aviv-Yafo, Tel-Aviv Museum, 50 Peintres de Renoir à Kisling, December 1964 – January 1965, no. 30. | Vevey, Musée Jenisch, De Vallotton à Desnos, July 24 - October 3, 1965, no. 29. | Geneva, Petit Palais Genève, Rétrospective 1910, le salon des indépendants de Paris, May 20 - June 20, 1969, no. 11. | Turin, Galleria d'Arte Pirra, Pointillisme, 1976, no. 6. | Dusseldorf, Städtische Kunsthalle, Vom Licht zur Farbe, May 27 – July 10, 1977, no. 22. | Berlin, Staatliche Kunsthalle, Die Gesellschaftliche Wirklichkeit der Kinder in der bildenden Kunst, December 16, 1979 – February 10, 1980, no. 140. | | Literature | I. Compin, H.E. Cross, Paris, 1964, no. 139 (illustrated p. 239). | F. Daulte, O. Ghez & E. Gibaudo, L'aube de XXe siècle de Renoir à Chagall, vol. I, Geneva, 1968, no. 96 (illustrated; titled 'L'enfant à la poupée'). | P. Offenstadt, Henri-Edmond Cross, Catalogue raisonné de l'oeuvre peint, Paris, 2022, no. 248 (illustrated p. 270). | | | | "In [Cross's] work one can sense the joy of painting, the love of delicate harmonies, an inexpressible hesitation, mystery and unexpectedness. He is at once a cold, methodical thinker, and a strange and troubled dreamer." | – Paul Signac | | Painted circa 1902-1905, l'Enfant au tablier blanc is a sublime example of Henri-Edmond Cross' signature Neo-Impressionist style. By this time, Cross had shifted away from his Pointillist technique, using broader brushstrokes, and leaving small areas of exposed, bare canvas visible between the strokes. The result is a shimmering mosaic of brilliant and pure color. Cross' Neo-Impressionist technique would influence artists such as Henri Matisse, André Derain and Henri Manguin, and was instrumental in forming the principles of Fauvism and later Cubism. | | Cross was captivated by the sumptuous colors and abundant vegetation of his own garden. Here, the garden is shown at the height of its growth. Cross has filled the canvas with layers of dense, blooming foliage. In the foreground, a young girl in a white apron sits, while behind her, a mother and young boy tend to the garden. Vibrant shades of green, blue, lavender, and yellow dance across the surface of the canvas in a densely woven tapestry of color, while interspersed are soft pinks and poppy red. In l'Enfant au tablier blanc, the fluidity and freedom of Cross's brushstroke is a direct result of his attempts to merge the chromatic principles of divisionism with a new expressiveness that reflected his own love of and excitement for the landscape. | | The first recorded owner of l'Enfant au tablier blanc was Oscar Ghez, a businessman and art collector. Alongside his brother, Ghez achieved success after establishing the first assembly lines of rubber boots and tire production. Due to mounting political tensions, their business moved from Rome to Lyon and ultimately to New York. During this time, Ghez was appointed as advisor for Italian affairs to the Pentagon due to his profound knowledge of Italy. | | In his leisure time, Ghez frequented antique shops, where he began collecting old books and Chinese porcelain and jade. After the death of his brother, this interest became more than a mere hobby and Ghez dedicated his time towards building his art collection. At first, Ghez focused on painters of Montmartre and the Belle Epoque but after several business trips to Paris, his interest shifted towards Neo- and Post-Impressionist and Fauvist works. Ghez was very selective in his acquisitions and would not let the opinions of others sway his choices. This instinct led him to discover master artists who were neglected at the time, such as Gustave Caillebotte, Charles Angrand and Louis Valtat, as well as female artists like Marie Bracquemond and Maria Blanchard. | | Ghez sold his factories in 1960; in 1965, he purchased a private mansion in Geneva. Three years later, he would open the Petit Palais de Genève, with the aim of exhibiting artists who had been overlooked by their contemporaries. Ghez's dedication to sharing art with the public extended not only to the Petit Palais, but to museums worldwide – with whom Ghez would frequently arrange traveling exhibitions. Such was the case with l'Enfant au tablier blanc, which during its time in Ghez's collection, was exhibited at institutions in cities around the world – including Turin, Berlin, Geneva and Tel Aviv.

title: Frères et soeurs du peintre
description: Frères et soeurs du peintre signed and dated 'Raoul Dufy Mai 1898,' and inscribed 'Henriette-Jean-Jeanne-Germaine' (lower right) watercolor on paper 19 5/8 x 24 3/8 in (49.9 x 61.9 cm) Executed in May 1898
provenance: Emilienne Dufy Collection, Nice (the artist's wife). | Jean-Claude Moloux Collection, Philadelphia (a gift from the above); his sale, Sotheby's Parke Bernet, New York, May 22, 1981, lot 814. | Acquired at the above sale by the previous owner; their sale, Christie's, New York, May 14, 2021, lot 476. | Acquired at the above sale by the present owner. | | Exhibited | Paris, Musée National d'Art Moderne, Raoul Dufy 1877-1953, June 26 – October 18, 1953. | Honfleur, Hôtel de Ville, Hommage à Raoul Dufy, July 3 – August 30, 1954, no. 1 (titled 'Henriette, Jean, Jeanne, Germaine'). | Eindhoven, Stedelijk Van Abbemuseum, Raoul Dufy, March 5 – April 24, 1955, no. 1. | Lyon, Musée de Lyon, Dufy, June 25 – October 13, 1957, no. 84. | | Literature | F. Guillon-Lafaille, Raoul Dufy, Catalogue raisonné des aquarelle, gouaches et pastels, vol. I, Paris, 1981, no. 1 (illustrated p. 2). | | | Painted in 1898 when Raoul Dufy was just 21 years old, Frères et sœurs du peintre is a rare surviving example of the artist's early work. In this watercolor, Dufy draws inspiration from his everyday life and depicts four of his eight siblings engaged in daily tasks. This intimate work features his siblings Henriette, Jean, Jeanne, and Germaine clad in blue and seated around a table with a red tablecloth. | | It was not until seeing Henri Matisse's Luxe, calme et volupté in 1905 that Dufy converted to Fauvism, but even while working in the Impressionist style, Dufy's interest in color is evident. In Frères et sœurs du peintre, the colors are not limited to a restrictive, carefully defined pattern. Rather, the colors are fluid and interact with neighboring tones to reveal their brilliance and promote a sense of unity throughout the composition. Utilizing the transparency of the watercolor and a variety of soft and cold tones, Dufy expertly evokes the world of childhood and the tender images he keeps of it. In this work, the slightly blurred touch achieved through broken brushstrokes and unblended colors allows Dufy to detach from realistic representation in favor of conveying impressions and feelings. The shades of blue and mauve dotted with touches of white perfectly capture the calm and studious atmosphere of the scene.

title: Un chat sur une palissade
description: Un chat sur une palissade signed 'Steinlen' (upper right) oil on canvas 21 3/8 x 25 1/2 in (54.3 x 64.8 cm) Painted in 1909
provenance: Y. Lamberty Collection, Paris, by 1920; his sale, Galerie Georges Giroux, Brussels, March 19-20, 1920, lot 187. | Georges Willems Collection, Brussels (acquired at the above sale). | Sale: Galerie Georges Giroux, Brussels, December 16, 1939, lot 71. | Meissner Collection, Zurich. | Roland, Browse & Delbanco, London. | Mrs. Dawson Collection. | Maynard Walker Gallery, New York. | Durlacher Brothers & Co., New York. | George H. Bunting & Karen Dean Bitler Bunting Collection, Kansas City (acquired from the above). | Lee & Mary Myers Collection, San Francisco (acquired from the above by June 1969). | Acquired from the above by the late owner in October 1969. | | | This work is part of the Ralph T. Coe Center for the Arts Collection, being sold in support of the Center's Restructuring Program. Proceeds from the sale will directly support the Coe Center's efforts to reunite Indigenous artworks with their origin communities. | | | | The feline creature is a prominent subject throughout Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen's prolific career. The Swiss-born French artist experimented with various depictions of the animal across a wide array of mediums, including lithographs, paintings, posters, and sculptures. | | In Un chat sur une palissade, Steinlen uses painstaking detail to capture the essence and personality of an aloof tabby cat draped gracefully across a wooden fence railing. The tabby's narrowed, yellow eyes blend in with the background foliage, bathing the entire composition in golden hues of light. While the artist was known to have a personal affection for cats and often fed local strays, the frequent presence of felines throughout his oeuvre was likely due to their symbolism of bohemia. Steinlen's Parisian neighborhood of Montmartre was often teeming with wild cats, which many took as a metaphor for modern bohemia or a rejection of bourgeois socio-political norms. As such, the artist's simplistic yet stylistically elegant illustrations would allow a direct and powerful delivery of his own political messages. As in the present work, the depiction of elegant, sophisticated cats, often in moments of leisure, allowed for the artist's political, humanitarian message to maintain a sense of empathy and intimacy in a way that set him apart from his Art Nouveau counterparts. | | Painted in 1909, the first earliest owner of Un chat sur une palissade was M.Y. Lamberty, a prolific Parisian collector who owned the painting by 1920. By 1969, the painting was acquired by the notable art collector Ralph Tracey "Ted" Coe (1929-2010), best known for his instrumental impact in the growth of appreciation of Native American art in the 20th century. As the Curator of Paintings and Sculpture at the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas City, Coe first discovered Un chat sur une palissade while advising Mrs. George H. Bunting, the volunteer director of the sales at the Nelson Gallery of Art, while on a trip to New York City. A memorable moment for the collector, Coe reflects upon his first encounter with the work: | | "I was shown a number of 17th-century paintings, and then out popped an early painting by Steinlen of the "Summer Cat" [Un chat sur une palissade], a painted version of one of his most famous color prints. This was not a lithograph, but a painting done at the same time as the print. Mrs. Bunting bought the painting for her daughter Karen, and years later... she wanted to sell the painting, and I acquired it from her. Ever since I have treasured this painting.... I still enjoy the tigerous touch of the background foliage and the cat's fur coat. The eyes are also full of feminine feistiness." | | Long prized as a jewel of Coe's private collection, Un chat sur une palissade, has remained in the Ralph T. Coe Center for the Arts since 2011, after being donated following the collector's death. | | Un chat sur une palissade (1909) was used as a study for the color lithograph entitled L'Été, chat sur une balustrade (Summer, Cat on a Balustrade). Lithographs from the original edition of 250 are in the permanent collections of many museums, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York and The Art Institute of Chicago in Illinois.

Clair (ed.), Balthus, exh. cat., Milan, 2001, no. 75 (illustrated p. 295). | | | Balthus was a reclusive artist whose distinctive style remains largely undefinable to this day. His self-described classicism resulted in highly enigmatic works, like Jeune fille à sa toilette, whose disquieting subjects lend to deep introspection. When art critic John Russell asked Balthus to provide introductory text for a retrospective held by the Tate Gallery in 1968, Balthus wrote: "The best way of starting is to say that Balthus is a painter about whom we know nothing. And now, let us look at his paintings" (the artist quoted in John Russel, Balthus- A Retrospective Exhibition, Tate Gallery, London, 1968, p. 7). | | The present work, painted in the latest stages of Balthus's career in 1948, represents an iconic culmination in the French artist's fascination with adolescence. Jeune fille à sa toilette, depicting a girl at the threshold of puberty, simultaneously exudes a sense of eroticism and empathy that generates a disquieting unease. The strict compositional order and stage-like interior setting, largely devoid of identifying elements, is typical of Balthus's oeuvre during the time spent in his studio at 3 cour de Rohan between 1948 and 1960. At this time, Balthus also began exploring a new physical type. | | As shown in Jeune fille à sa toilette, this new model is extremely young, thick-set, and appears almost androgynous in bodily form. The ostensibly unselfconscious girl rests her hand on the back of a chair, posing confidently and gazing unflinchingly into the eyes of the viewer. The room offers little evidence of the real world, and the young girl remains completely isolated save for the elderly woman shown in profile. The motif of the elderly attendant or maid figure reappeared continuously throughout the work of Balthus with the intention, many believed, of further emphasizing the seclusion of the young girl. The narrative of the present toilette scene is ambiguous, presumably by choice. The older woman waits at a distance in the back of the compositional space, holding a towel at the ready for the young girl standing at her dressing table. It is presumed by many that the elderly woman represents the housekeeper character in Emily Brontë's novel Wuthering Heights of 1848. The artist would have been exposed to such a literary influence after executing a series of illustrations for the English classic between the years of 1932 and 1935 (idea referenced in Carandente, Balthus, Drawings and Watercolours, London, 1983, p. 47). | | Jeune fille à sa toilette comes to auction with a storied, impressive exhibition history. Speaking to the significance of this work in connection with the oeuvre of Balthus, Jeune fille à sa toilette has been exhibited at Balthus retrospective exhibitions across the world. Highlights include the Museum of Modern Art (New York), The Tate Gallery (London), the Musée National d'Art Moderne (Paris), and the Palazzo Grassi (Venice).

description: Pendants Pending inscribed 'Man Ray' and stamped with two hallmarks (on the inside of each earring) pair of gold-plated silver earrings in a leather presentation box with blue velvet-lined interior 5 5/16 in (13.5 cm) (length) Conceived and executed in 1967 in an edition of 4 examples plus artist's proofs. The present example may be an artist's proof
provenance: Private collection; their sale, Sotheby's, New York, April 24, 1981, lot 203. | Acquired at the above sale by the present owner. | | Literature | B. Hermann, J.-H. Martin & R. Krauss, Man Ray, Objets de mon affection, sculptures et objects, Catalogue raisonné, Paris, 1983, p. 163 (another example illustrated). | | | In the 1960s, American surrealist artist Man Ray collaborated with the Italian jewelry production firm Gem Montebello to create jewelry. Looking to a design he created for Lampshade (Abat-Jour) in 1919, Man Ray designed these eye-catching, oversized earrings to be produced in Milan by GianCarlo Montebello, a fabricator who had asked some of the 20th-century's most notable artists to apply their skills to jewelry. In addition to painting and design, Man Ray was a highly respected photographer and, therefore, was heavily involved in the creative process of photographing his jewelry designs. In his shoots, Man Ray would often incorporate photos of celebrities and socialites wearing his jewelry creations. In 1966, Man Ray photographed French actress Catherine Deneuve wearing the spiraling 'Pendantif-Pendant' earrings. In the shoot, a young Deneuve is pictured surrounded by objects harvested from the artist's studio while adorned with the gold-plated Pendants Pending earrings. Here, the jewelry forms a dialogue with geometric and organic shapes juxtaposed alongside his other creations positioned around the model, whose slightly wavy hair seems to echo the delicate twist of the precious metal.

title: Paisaje surrealista
description: Paisaje surrealista signed and dated 'Carreño - 70' (lower left) oil on canvas 25 5/16 x 31 5/16 in (64.3 x 79.6 cm) Painted in 1970
provenance: Private collection, Miami. | Sale: Christie's, New York, November 21, 1990, lot 214. | Acquired at the above sale by the previous owner. | Thence by descent to the present owner. | | | Mario Carreño Morales (known as Mario Carreño), is widely recognized as one of the most distinguished exponents of 20th Century Latin American painting. His constantly evolving life's work furthered nearly every major artistic movement of the century and is notable for harmonious compositions, chromatic sensuality, impeccable technique, and lyrical expressiveness. Born in Havana, where he was a member of the legendary Origenes (nativist-baroque) movement, thereafter he lived intermittently in Mexico City, Madrid, Paris, and New York (he taught painting at the New School in New York City from 1942-44). Ultimately, he spent the final 40-plus years of his life as a citizen of Chile, marrying there the painter Ida Gonzalez, Pablo Neruda's amanuensis at the time. In the mid-1960s, deeply afflicted by world events, Carreño's thematics evolved from a purely geometric abstraction into a poetic synthesis of surreal, metaphysical, and geometric humanism, placed within a silent Chilean geography – coastal, sparse, and mountainous. Paisaje surrealista, from 1970, is one of Carreño's earliest completed paintings in the new aesthetic, and is representative of the mature style in works like Atardecer de la nostalgia and La caida de los grandes mitos. The elegant folds of drapery and balanced composition inject classical and renaissance elements, recalling earlier works such as Desnudos con mangos and El nacimiento de las naciones americanas, while here the voluptuous figures, truncated and silhouetted, inhabit a dream-like, post-modern landscape. | | Carreño's paintings are held by prominent museums such as the National Museums of Chile, Uruguay, Venezuela, Argentina, and Cuba, the New York and San Francisco Museums of Modern Art, and the Art Museum of the Americas, Washington, D.C..

title: Cheval galopant
description: Cheval galopant stamped with the artist's signature (Lugt 658; lower left) black pencil on paper 9 5/16 x 12 7/16 in (23.6 x 31.6 cm) Executed circa 1880
provenance: Atelier Edgar Degas, Paris; his Estate sale, Galerie Georges Petit, Paris, 4th sale, July 2-4, 1919, lot 234c. | Jean Lonchamp Collection, Paris; his sale, Binoche Renaud-Giquello & Associés, Paris, March 25, 2022, lot 38. | Acquired at the above sale by the present owner. | | | Horses and the racetrack fascinated Edgar Degas and were a prominent recurring theme throughout his art. While Degas never rode horses himself, he frequently attended horse races and began sketching studies of racehorses as an art student. As a young artist, Degas drew inspiration from the depiction of horses in paintings by Theodore Gericault (1791-1824) and Gustave Moreau (1826-1898). As Degas' technical skill improved however, he was no longer concerned with simply capturing the horse's anatomy, but rather, how these graceful thoroughbreds moved through space. Degas' interest in capturing the complexity of racehorses in motion, which began in the 1880s, was likely a direct result of Eadweard Muybridge's acclaimed photographic studies of horses in motion. By devising the first 'automatic' camera shutter, Muybridge was able to capture the sheer force and elegance of a galloping racehorse through a series of photographs taken in rapid succession. In the present drawing, Degas employed black pencil to capture the exact moment when all four hooves of the horse have left the ground. This split second of time, known as a transverse gallop, is nearly undetectable by the human eye and was the original driving force behind Muybridge's photographic studies of the equine form. Likely used as a preliminary study for a painting, Cheval galopant is an excellent example of Degas' interest in capturing fleeting moments from urban life.

title: Madame Vuillard en peignoir rouge
description: Madame Vuillard en peignoir rouge stamped with the artist's signature 'E Vuillard' (lower right) oil on canvas 26 1/4 x 21 15/16 in (66.7 x 55.8 cm) Painted circa 1911
provenance: The artist's studio. | Charles-Auguest Girard Collection, Paris. | Private collection, Paris. | | Literature | A. Salomon & G. Cogeval, Vuillard, The Inexhaustible Glance, Critical Catalogue of Paintings and Pastels, vol. II, Paris, 2003, no. IX-39, (illustrated p. 1049). | | | Painted circa 1911, Madame Vuillard en peignoir rouge was created at the height of Vuillard's career, a time during which the artist enjoyed both critical and commercial success. Unburdened by financial constraints, Vuillard was free to paint his preferred subjects, and he turned to those closest to him. The present painting continues the subject matter of his earlier Nabis paintings, where, in contrast to the preferred esoteric subjects of the other Nabis members to communicate their Synthetist visions, Vuillard turned to the domestic. It was through mundane observations, Vuillard believed, that latent mystery and sentiment were revealed. In 1893, Vuillard expressed this notion in his journal when posing the rhetorical question: "Why is it in the familiar places that the mind and sensibility find the greatest degree of genuine novelty?" (E. Vuillard quoted in B. Thomson, Vuillard, Oxford, 1988, p. 44). | | Seated in a yellow and green armchair, Madame Vuillard is depicted here within the cluttered Clichy apartment, surrounded by the oriental rug, patterned textiles, and richly upholstered furniture so typical of the bourgeois salons of France's Third Republic. Despite her central positioning, little attention is given to Madame Vuillard's physiognomy, and she is depicted with the same energized brushwork that Vuillard employs throughout the composition. This formal simplification and lack of detail was in accordance with the Nabis' philosophy which sought to represent a symbolic distillation of experience. Consequently, a faithful representation of the subject was suppressed to heighten the emotional import of the composition. As Vuillard explained, "a woman's head just produced in me a certain emotion, I must make use of this emotion alone and I must not try to remember the nose or the ear, they're of no importance" (E. Vuillard quoted in B. Thomson, ibid, p. 28). | | Even at a time when the prevailing Avant-Garde, notably the Fauves, began to experiment with idyllic and Arcadian themes, Vuillard remained steadfast to genre subjects, particularly domestic scenes, throughout his career. Madame Vuillard en peignoir rouge is a testament to Vuillard's enduring fascination with quotidian, intimate spaces where, by returning to those most familiar to him, he was able to fully explore the formal potential of his compositions.

The deep brown hues of the vase contrast against the pure colors of white, blue, green and yellow seen within the finely rendered flowers. The diverse use of rich color - executed in delicate and soft brushstrokes set against the muted, earthy tones of the background - gives the illusion of depth and situates the arrangement in time and place. | | Vlaminck's use of color and powerful brushstrokes during the height of his Fauve years had a lasting effect on modern art, inspiring specific Expressionist movements such as Die Brucke, Blaue Reiter and Neo-Fauvism. The French poet and art critic Guillaume Apollinaire once referred to Vlaminck as "one of the most talented painters of his generation. His simple and intensive technique allows the lines their full liberty, the volumes their full relief, and the colors their full clarity, their full beauty."
